KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Due to high monthly astronomical tides, water levels will 
continue to be high during each high tide cycle thru the 
weekend. Storm surge it just beginning to increase after being
near zero with high tide this afternoon. However by midday Fri 
astronomical tides will be coming down but storm surge will be 
higher. Confidence would be slightly higher at water levels well
into minor flood stage if winds were more onshore, but 
alongshore winds are likely and will still drive a storm surge 
towards the coast. Surge values roughly around 1 ft will bring 
us just over minor flood stage with waves building to around 10 
ft. Plus as you move southwest along the coast towards the 
Seacoast, winds will have more of an onshore component. Coastal
Flood Advisory remain in effect for the midday Fri high tide. 
Aside from the minor flooding Fri, beach erosion and overwash 
can be anticipated.

Guidance can also sometimes be too quick to lower storm surge 
behind a departing storm, especially if winds do not quickly 
turn offshore. So we continue to monitor trends for the the Sat
high tide.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

High pressure continues to slowly retreat thru this evening
allowing clouds to lower and thicken and rain to creep steadily
northward. Temps have struggled to warm much thru the thick
cirrus and developing cold air damming so I have adjusted those
down. A myriad of hazards are possible so I will cover those
below in order of confidence.

Wind: The potent easterly LLJ is battering the Mid Atlantic with
numerous 50 to 60 mph gusts. This is forecast to weaken as the
storm lifts north and occludes tonight. Despite that winds will
still be gusty, especially along the coast and for portions of
southwestern and western NH. Aside from 35 to 45 mph gusts along
the Seacoast to Saco Bay, the inversion height aloft is well
positioned to be near summit level from the Monadnocks north
into the Sunapee region. The pressure gradient across the
terrain will help accelerate what is left of the LLJ down the
lee slopes. So a narrow band of 50+ mph gusts is in the forecast
for these areas. It is just so localized that a Wind Advisory
did not make sense to me. The power outage threat is limited,
and will mainly be due to shaking out the deadfall after leaf
drop. Once the LLJ lifts north of the area by Fri morning winds
will drop off pretty quickly.

Freezing Rain/Ice: As usual the cold air damming is looking a
little stronger than modeling. I have already adjusted temps
down thru Fri using hi-res guidance. Fri has some real potential
to be much cooler than guidance, with a lack of northwest winds
to mix out the lower level cold air. To the north there is a  
more wet bulb cooling potential, but if dewpoints continue to 
creep up into the mid to upper 20s even those locations should 
be relatively safe from ice. It is possible there is some brief 
freezing rain before flipping to rain, especially across the 
southern foothills. More likely will be that the foothills and 
mtns remain at or below freezing and stay there longer. So ice 
amounts did come up just a bit, with more areas across the 
western Maine mtns around a tenth of an inch of ice. But the 
temp trends this evening will have to be watched closely. Rain 
will be falling onto bare pavement, some of which is untreated 
this early in the season, and besides the latent heating from 
freezing there is not much of a reason for temps to budge 
overnight. So once we lock in, that is where it could stay thru 
morning. The Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect for 
slippery roads.

Rain: Rainfall amounts remain the lowest confidence part of the
forecast. Most of the rain falls in little more than 6 hours at
any given location overnight followed by a large dry slot. It
may remain damp or drizzly, but serious rainfall accumulation
will be done once that moves in. Hi-res guidance continues to
highlight the Seacoast up to Casco Bay for totals greater than
an inch, likely incorporating coastal front enhancement.
Sometimes hi-res guidance likes to overdo this and it will be
hard to see much more than that in 6 hours. After a period of
mist or drizzle the upper low begins to rotate overhead and an
area of showers is likely to drift across the forecast area Fri
evening into early Sat. After that flow turns northwesterly and
true upslope rain and snow showers begin.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

A weak wave aloft could bring a few rain or snow showers Saturday 
night, but otherwise we'll see drier weather for Sunday as high 
pressure builds overhead. Temperatures are expected to remain above 
normal for Sunday with highs in the 40s to low 50s.

There's good agreement in model guidance for a quick-hitting system 
to bring another round of precipitation Sunday night into Monday.
